results.title: Controlling your type I errors: Bonferroni and Benjamini-Hochberg
results.content: Under the advanced settings of any experiment on Statsig, you can select whether you want to use the Bonferroni Correction or a Benjamini-Hochberg Procedure. Like with a Bonferroni Correction, when you apply the Benjamini-Hochberg Procedure in Statsig you can decide whether to apply the method per variant, per metric, or both. When we apply the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure based on the number of metrics, we are controlling the FDR using the above method for each variant independent of the others. Similarly, when we apply the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure based on the number of variants, we control the FDR using the above method for each metric independent of the others. When we apply the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure based on number of metrics and variants, we control the FDR for the whole experiment by applying the above method for all the p-values for each metric and variant together. results.title: Benjamini-Hochberg Correction - MetricGate Calculator
results.content: Try our Benjamini-Hochberg Calculator to control the false discovery rate in your multiple hypothesis tests. # Benjamini-Hochberg Procedure (False Discovery Rate Control). The Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure is a powerful method for controlling the False Discovery Rate (FDR) in multiple hypothesis testing. Unlike the Bonferroni or Holm corrections, which control the probability of any false positives (family-wise error rate), the BH procedure focuses on controlling the expected proportion of false positives among all rejected hypotheses. Suppose you run *m* hypothesis tests and obtain p-values *p(1), ..., p(m)* sorted in ascending order. 2. For each p-value *p(i)*, calculate the threshold: \dfrac{i}{m} \cdot \alpha. The BH procedure is especially suited to exploratory research and large-scale testing scenarios where FDR control is more appropriate than family-wise error rate control. Suppose you have six p-values:. With \alpha = 0.05 and *m = 6* tests, the BH threshold for each rank *i* is \dfrac{i}{6} \cdot 0.05. # Benjamini-Hochberg FDR Correction Example in R # Simulated p-values from 6 hypothesis tests raw_pvalues <- c(0.005, 0.01, 0.04, 0.08, 0.12, 0.20) # Apply BH correction bh_adjusted <- p.adjust(raw_pvalues, method = "BH") # Compile results results <- data.frame( Test = paste0("H", 1:6), Raw_P = raw_pvalues, BH_Adjusted_P = round(bh_adjusted, 3), Significant = bh_adjusted < 0.05 ) # Print results print(results) # Optional visualization barplot( bh_adjusted, names.arg = results$Test, col = ifelse(results$Significant, "red", "gray"), ylab = "Adjusted P-value", main = "Benjamini-Hochberg Adjusted P-values" ) abline(h = 0.05, col = "blue", lty = 2) legend("topright", legend = c("Significant", "Not Significant"), fill = c("red", "gray")). After applying the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure, two hypotheses (H1 and H2) are flagged as statistically significant at the 5% FDR threshold. * **Significant:** H1 and H2 have BH-adjusted p-values of 0.03 → we reject the null hypothesis for these comparisons, controlling the expected proportion of false discoveries. * **Not Significant:** H3 to H6 have adjusted p-values between 0.08 and 0.20 → we do not reject their null hypotheses. This demonstrates the strength of BH correction: it allows more discoveries (H1 and H2) than stricter methods like Bonferroni, while still controlling the false discovery rate across all comparisons. * **Does not guarantee zero false positives:** It controls the proportion, not the presence, of false discoveries.

results.title: Benjamini-Hochberg correction: reducing false positives in testing
results.content: # Benjamini-Hochberg correction: reducing false positives in testing. Ever felt overwhelmed by the sheer number of tests you're running and worried about stumbling upon false positives? In this blog, we'll dive into the challenges of multiple testing and how it can lead to false positives. More importantly, we'll explore how the **Benjamini-Hochberg correction** can help manage these false discoveries, and how tools like Statsig make this process smoother. ## The challenge of multiple testing and false positives. The **Benjamini-Hochberg correction**, for example, controls the false discovery rate (FDR). So, let's talk about the **Bonferroni correction**—it's like the old-school way to keep false positives (Type I errors) in check when you're juggling multiple hypotheses. Instead of controlling the Family-Wise Error Rate (FWER) like Bonferroni does, it focuses on controlling the **false discovery rate (FDR)**. This approach offers a much better balance between catching true positives and limiting false ones, especially when you're handling large-scale testing. ## Introducing the Benjamini-Hochberg correction for managing false discoveries. Here's how it works: Instead of just slashing your significance threshold across the board, the Benjamini-Hochberg method ranks all your p-values from smallest to largest. By focusing on controlling the **FDR**, this method ensures that the proportion of false positives among all the significant results stays within limits you're comfortable with. Using the Benjamini-Hochberg correction lets you balance the need to discover real effects without getting bogged down by too many false discoveries. ## Implementing the Benjamini-Hochberg correction in your experiments. Next, for each p-value, you calculate a threshold: take your desired **false discovery rate (FDR)**, divide it by the total number of tests, and multiply by the rank of that p-value. The beauty of the Benjamini-Hochberg correction is how it balances catching real effects with keeping false discoveries in check—perfect when you're up against a mountain of hypotheses. Platforms like Statsig make it easy to incorporate the Benjamini-Hochberg correction into your workflow. Handling multiple tests without getting swamped by false positives is a real challenge, but tools like the **Benjamini-Hochberg correction** make it manageable. If you're keen to dive deeper, check out resources on multiple comparisons and false discovery rates.

results.title: How to use Bonferroni correction for multiple hypothesis testing
results.content: For instance, if you're running 20 tests with a significance level of 0.05, there's a whopping 64% chance of seeing at least one false positive without any correction. By adjusting our significance level using methods like the Bonferroni correction, we can keep the FWER at the desired level. Enter the Bonferroni correction—a simple yet powerful tool to adjust significance levels and reduce the risk of false positives in multiple comparisons. This gives you the **Bonferroni-corrected p-value threshold** (α/m), ensuring the family-wise error rate (FWER) stays controlled at your desired level. Just divide your desired significance level (α) by the number of comparisons to get the Bonferroni-corrected p-value threshold. By adjusting p-values for multiple comparisons, you can make more informed decisions based on reliable statistical evidence—avoiding the pitfalls of false positives. By allowing a small proportion of false positives, the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure is less conservative than the Bonferroni correction and more powerful in detecting true positives.

results.title: Benjamini–Hochberg Procedure | Statsig Docs
results.content: Benjamini–Hochberg Procedure | Statsig Docs The Benjamini-Hochberg Procedure ("BH" procedure) is a statistical method that reduces the probability of false positives by adjusting the significance level for multiple comparisons. It is not as extreme as a Bonferroni Correction, because instead of controlling the chance of at least one false positive (Family Wise Error Rate), BH controls the expected value of false positives when the null hypothesis has been rejected (False Discovery Rate). Like with many other analysis settings, you can enable BH procedure for individual experiments (or configure global Experiment Settings to default it). : Benjamini-Hochberg procedure configuration interface The Benjamini-Hochberg Procedure updates the significance level to be used (modifying your pre-set α\alpha α). The new significance level to be applied is calculated by sorting the p-values of metrics in ascending order and comparing with a paired threshold. Each p-value’s paired threshold is the desired False Discovery Rate divided by the number of comparisons being evaluated multiplied by what rank a p-value is in the ordered list. The largest threshold value which is higher than its corresponding p-value is our new significance level (α\alpha α). The Benjamini-Hochberg Procedure can be applied based on: * The number of test groups (multiple treatment hypotheses). For each metric aggregate the list of p-values from each variant and complete the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure. * The number of metrics in the scorecard. For each variant aggregate the list of p-values from each metric and complete the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure. * Both the number of test groups and number of metrics in the scorecard. All p-values are aggregated to complete the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure. Statsig does not apply BH procedure when evaluating the p-values of any event-dimension or user-property experiment metric results. Only the top-line metric results are compared to the new significance level. Last updated on **Sep 18, 2025**
